title: No Air in Space. So What Does a Rocket Push On? | How It Works #6
simplified: Simplified model: gas pressure shown as arrows on the chamber walls; the speed meter is illustrative of a climb to orbit, not a real flight profile.

hook_candidates.text: Up here, there's no air. So what's this rocket pushing on?
This rocket has nothing to push against. Watch it speed up anyway.
You push off a wall to swim. A rocket has no wall.
Rockets work better with no air at all.
Seal this rocket's nozzle, and it goes nowhere. Why?

parts.text: So what's this rocket pushing on?
Orbit needs twenty eight thousand kilometres an hour.
parts.tts: Orbit needs twenty-eight thousand kilometres an hour.

parts.text: and the hot gas pushes every wall equally.
so nothing cancels the push on the front.
Air only gets in the way.
the same engine pushes even harder.
parts.tts: the same engine pushes even harder!

sources: Orbit speed: 'The speed required for an object to go into space and orbit the Earth (orbital velocity) is about 28,000 km/hr (17,500 mph) at low earth orbit.' Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, Ask an Explainer, https://howthingsfly.si.edu/ask-an-explainer/what-speed-required-launch-object-space

Sealed vs open: in a closed balloon 'the inward and outward pressing forces are balanced'; 'When the nozzle is released, air escapes through it and the balloon is propelled in the opposite direction.' NASA Glenn Research Center, Rocket Principles, https://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/k-12/rocket/TRCRocket/rocket_principles.html

Air gets in the way / pushes harder in space: 'rockets actually work better in space than they do in air.' 'In space, the exhaust gases can escape freely.' NASA Glenn, Rocket Principles (above). Thrust equation F = mdot*Ve + (pe - p0)*Ae: lower outside pressure p0 gives more thrust. NASA Glenn, Rocket Thrust Equation, https://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/K-12/airplane/rockth.html

Pushing against its own exhaust: 'For every action there is always an opposite and equal reaction' (Newton's third law), NASA Glenn, Rocket Principles; rockets 'can generate thrust in a vacuum', NASA Glenn, Rocket Thrust Equation.
comment_question: Before this, what did you think a rocket pushed against in space?
